terms.gloss: the fact, the facts, what really is (as against words or opinion)
evidence: Cic. Tusc. 5.32: rem enim opīnor spectārī oportēre, nōn verba
Traupman 97: rēs ipsa indicat, the facts speak for themselves
terms.comment: Lewis & Short sets it against verba, opīniō and nōmen.

terms.grammar: phrase: ablative of rēs with vērus
terms.comment: Sometimes written as one word, rēvērā (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. Att. 2.4.1: fēcistī mihi pergrātum, quod Serāpiōnis librum ad mē mīsistī
Ter. Eun. 5.4.19: dicta et facta (Lewis & Short, s.v. faciō)
terms.comment: Not a fact in the modern sense: classically a deed or an exploit, and factum est means “it was done, it happened”.

phrases.latin: rem enim opīnor spectārī oportēre, nōn verba
phrases.english: for I think it is the facts that should be looked at, not the words

phrases.latin: Piscēs illī, quī annō tōtō in memoriā ejus crēverant, rē vērā nōn minōrēs appāruērunt
phrases.english: Those fish, which had grown in his memory all year, turned out in fact to be no smaller
phrases.source: Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium

phrases.latin: fēcistī mihi pergrātum, quod Serāpiōnis librum ad mē mīsistī
phrases.english: it was very kind of you to send me Serapio’s book

sources: Lewis & Short: res · Lewis & Short: quod · Lewis & Short: facio
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 97, 312.
Quotations of Cicero’s letters (Purser) and the Tusculans (Pohlenz) that are not in the loci collections were checked against the Perseus Latin texts (9 November 2026).
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
Theodōrus et pater · Ad Larem avītum, Libellī I–VII, as they stood on 9 November 2026. Examples marked “Libellus” quote those texts word for word.
